20.0.0.en: 1 Then answered Zophar the Naamathite, and said, 2 Therefore do my thoughts cause me to answer, and for this I make haste. 3 I have heard the check of my reproach, and the spirit of my understanding causeth me to answer.

20.0.1.en: Then answered Zophar the Naamathite, and said [1]:

20.1.0.en: Therefore do my thoughts cause me to answer, and for this I make haste [2].

20.1.1.en: It seems that Zophar was greatly offended by what Job had said, and thought that he was justifying himself although Zophar was sure of his wickedness.

20.1.2.en: Zophar was vexed that Job spoke of his hope in heaven and of salvation as though he were a righteous and good man. So he attacked him violently, saying that his thoughts drove him to not remain silent about what Job had said, but to be obliged to answer him.

20.1.3.en: Zophar confessed that anxious thoughts had filled his mind and that agitation had mastered him. Perhaps here he expresses the inner turmoil and anger within himself and within his two companions. This anger stops the ears from hearing the truth, and the eyes from seeing the truth however plain it may be, so that they saw in Job nothing but a mass of hidden evils, covered with hypocrisy, false giving and feigned tenderness. This is what drove Zophar to biting criticism and harsh rebuke, and bitter threats of the evils that would befall Job.

20.1.4.en: * Anger lets the tongues loose and makes speech uncontrolled. Physical violence, acts of ridicule, abuse, accusations, beating and countless other evil deeds are born of anger and wrath.

20.1.5.en: St. Basil the Great * The sick mind does not control its judgments, and so it thinks that everything anger suggests to it is right.

20.1.7.en: I have heard the check of my reproach.

20.2.0.en: And the spirit of my understanding causeth me to answer [3].

20.2.1.en: "I have heard the check of my reproach" is rendered by some: "I have heard you repel my rebuke."

20.2.2.en: They counted Job's words an insult, and that he was not worthy of their speaking to him or offering him counsel. Perhaps they had set it in their hearts to stop the dialogue, because it is of no use with an evil man like this. But Zophar's heart provoked him greatly, so he was compelled to speak.

20.3.s.en: 2. The success of the wicked is temporary

20.3.0.en: 4 Knowest thou not this of old, since man was placed upon earth, 5 That the triumphing of the wicked is short, and the joy of the hypocrite but for a moment? 6 Though his excellency mount up to the heavens, and his head reach unto the clouds; 7 Yet he shall perish for ever like his own dung: they which have seen him shall say, Where is he? 8 He shall fly away as a dream, and shall not be found: yea, he shall be chased away as a vision of the night. 9 The eye also which saw him shall see him no more; neither shall his place any more behold him.

20.3.1.en: Knowest thou not this of old, since man was placed upon earth: [4]

20.3.2.en: Zophar resorted to Job's own knowledge before the trials came upon him, counting that it matched what they were saying to him, whereas now he objects to it and rejects it. It is a fixed principle that Job himself used to repeat before, and the experiences of the generations have confirmed it from of old. This truth is engraved in the mind of every man since the beginning of creation: the wickedness of the wicked destroys them.

20.3.3.en: * "Knowest thou not this of old, since man was placed upon earth?" By saying it in this manner Zophar abused Job, counting him ignorant of this truth (or ignoring it), although Job had declared it in particular in his next statement.

20.3.4.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * It is clear that Zophar, puffed up with his knowledge, distorted the statements he made against the wicked, since his aim was to rebuke blessed Job. For he saw that Job had walked first in the straight ways and afterward suffered punishment, and so he counted all that he had seen before to have been practised by Job as a form of hypocrisy, for he did not believe that a righteous servant could fall into distress by a just God.

20.3.6.en: What have we received since the fall of our first parents, Adam and Eve, except that we need the work of God, to tear down all evil in us, and to build all that befits His righteousness? So we should not wonder if God's call to His men is to root out and destroy, and to throw down the wicked peoples and corrupt kingdoms, which point to evil, in order to build and to plant what belongs to God, as it was said to the prophet Jeremiah at his call to service (Jer 1:10). Evil must be torn down for righteousness to stand; and if the wicked persist in clinging to evil, they perish with the evil.

20.3.7.en: We have no choice except between two things, with no third: either our depths are a divine garden bearing the fruit of the Holy Spirit that gladdens the heart of God, or a playground for the enemy of good to lie in and dwell. Either our hearts are a temple in which the Holy Spirit dwells, or a stage on which the enemy of good practises his evils!

20.3.8.en: * "To root out, and to pull down" (Jer 1:10). There is a building of Satan and there is a building of God. The building "upon the sand" is of Satan, because it is not founded on anything solid and firm, but the building "upon a rock" is of God. See what is said to the believers: "Ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building" (1 Cor 3:9).

20.3.9.en: So the word of God is directed [to the nations and to the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down]. If we root out and do not destroy the thing rooted out, that thing remains; and if we pull down but do not remove the foundation stones, what was pulled down still remains. It is a mark of God's goodness and love that after He roots out, He destroys, and after He pulls down, He wipes out what has been pulled down.

20.3.10.en: As for the things rooted out and destroyed, read carefully how they are destroyed: [Burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire, and gather the tares to be burned, and cast them into the fire](a). This is the manner of wiping out and destruction after the rooting out. Would you also see the destruction that comes upon corrupt buildings after they are pulled down? That house which was pulled down because of leprosy turns to dust, and then this dust is taken and cast outside the city (Lev 14:41), so that not one stone remains(b), as in the saying: [I will beat them small as the dirt in the streets](c), or (I will level them with the ground).

20.3.11.en: Corrupt things must not remain at all; rather they are destroyed to avoid using their remains in building new buildings that Satan makes, and corrupt things are rooted out so that Satan may not find in them other seeds to plant again; therefore they are destroyed, that there may be no opportunity for Satan to sow tares among the wheat...

20.3.12.en: Therefore the first thing is that we uproot and pluck out all that is evil from our souls; for God cannot build where there are corrupt and evil buildings. [For what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?](d) Evil must be rooted out from its foundation. The building of the evil one must be pulled down completely from our souls, so that the words of God may do the work of building and planting in us.

20.3.13.en: For I cannot understand that statement in any other way: "Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth"(e). Why? "To root out, and to pull down, and to destroy"(e). Yes, they are words that root out nations. Words to pull down kingdoms, but not the material kingdoms of this world; rather you must understand in a lofty way what is meant by the words that root out and the words that pull down.

20.3.14.en: And then power is granted from God, as it is written: [The Lord giveth the word: great was the company of those that published it](f), a power that roots out whatever unbelief (hypocrisy) or vice it meets. A power that destroys and pulls down if idols are found set up inside the heart, so that when the idol is pulled down a temple of the Lord is set up in its place, and in this temple the glory of God is seen and appears, and tares no longer grow, but a paradise of God in the temple of God, in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

20.3.15.en: Origen How great is the difference between the planting of the enemy of good and the planting of the Lord, and between the building of the devil and the building of the Holy Spirit. The enemy of good sows grass, which appears quickly and dries quickly, and its portion is the fire. And the planting of the Lord is calm; He plants His Cross, the tree of life, in us, plants it by the streams of the Holy Spirit's waters, it bears fruit, and its fruit is eternal.

20.3.16.en: The success of the wicked is swift and temporary, but the success of the righteous is hidden, for trials surround them so that their crowns may shine all the more, and they may become bright stars accompanying the Sun of Righteousness in the very heaven.

20.4.0.en: That the triumphing of the wicked is short, and the joy of the hypocrite but for a moment! [5]

20.4.1.en: The triumph of the wicked will not last. They exult, but only for moments, then their shouting turns to wailing and lamentation. The wicked may prosper and feel secure, and you see them triumphant and glad, boasting of their wealth, power, greatness and success, but all this is for a time, and soon passes away in this world.

20.4.2.en: This principle is sound, but God has His judgments and dispensations, which differ with each person according to what is for his edification. On the other hand, Zophar was not pure in thought, nor was he defending a particular theological principle; most likely all he meant was to affirm Job's wickedness.

20.4.3.en: * "The mirth of the wicked is a sign of falling, and the joy of the hypocrite is destruction!" [5 LXX]. Zophar speaks in this statement with impudence, for he abuses Job severely and slanders him as his other two friends did. He blackened his reputation for the following reason: from the beginning, since the human race has existed, there has been joy and mirth over the fall of the wicked, and destruction for the ungodly, among whom is Job, as Zophar saw.

20.4.4.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem The wicked lose not only their passing worldly joy, but even the earth grieves and mourns (Jer 12:4), and nature groans because of them, and heaven too with its angels grieves over them. This is the effect of evil, which deprives man of true joy, and because of it many groan over him.

20.4.5.en: * "How long shall the land mourn, and the herbs of every field wither, for the wickedness of them that dwell therein?" (Jer 12:4). The prophet speaks here as though the earth were a living being, saying that it mourns because of the wickedness of those who walk upon it.

20.4.6.en: For each one of us the earth is either mourning because of our wickedness or rejoicing because of our virtues. And what is said of the earth is said without doubt of all things. Likewise I can say that the angel in charge of the water (as an example) rejoices or mourns; we must know that for the whole universe to be ordered and administered, there is an angel in charge of the earth, another in charge of the water, another of the air and another of the fire. Lift up your mind to contemplate the order prevailing among the animals, the plants and the heavenly bodies; there is an angel in charge even of the sun, another of the moon, and others of the stars.

20.4.7.en: All these angels who accompany us throughout our life on earth either rejoice for us or mourn over us when we sin.

20.4.8.en: Jeremiah says that the earth mourns because of those who dwell in it: by the word "earth" he means the angel dwelling in it, for it was also said: "But the idol made with hands is cursed, as well as he that made it" (Wis 14:8), not that the curse falls on the lifeless thing itself, but by the word "idol" he means the devil dwelling in it, who takes the "idol" as his name. In the same way I can say that "earth" means the angel in charge of the earth, and "water" the angel in charge of the water, of which it is written: [The waters saw thee, O God, the waters saw thee; they were afraid: the depths also were troubled. The clouds poured out water: the skies sent out a sound: thine arrows also went abroad] (Ps 77:17-18).

20.4.9.en: * You, O sinner, must taste now this extreme bitterness that God brings upon you, so that you may turn back from your way and be saved.

20.5.0.en: Origen Though his excellency mount up to the heavens, and his head reach unto the clouds [6]

20.5.1.en: Zophar supposed that the success of the wicked man had reached a height that no one could imagine, rising even to heaven. And if he grew until it seemed that his head touched the clouds, such would be his loftiness and arrogance that no one would think of a man approaching him or taking a stand of resistance toward him.

20.5.2.en: * If you have committed a sin, your adversary is the word of God... It is the enemy of your will until the Word becomes the security of your salvation. What a saving and helping enemy!

20.5.3.en: St. Augustine Yet he shall perish for ever like his own dung.

20.6.0.en: They which have seen him shall say, Where is he? [7]

20.6.1.en: He who attains all this greatness perishes like his own dung (his excrement or manure). Those who were amazed at his indescribable greatness look at him, and behold, he is not there; he has perished completely! All that remains is his smell, which cannot be borne or endured.

20.6.2.en: * It is said of the pride of the hypocrite that it lifts him to heaven, as his haughty thought seems to lead him to the heavenly life. It is as though his head had reached the clouds, when the leading member, his thinking mind, is supposed to be equal to the merits of the saints who went before him. But [he shall perish at last like a dunghill], because at his death, when he is led to torments, being full of the dung of evil habits, he falls under the feet of the evil spirits. For the delights of the present life, which the wicked think a great good, the righteous look upon as dung. Therefore it is written: [A slothful man is pelted with the dung of oxen] (Sir 22:2). For whoever does not follow God becomes sluggish in the love of eternal life...

20.6.3.en: "They which have seen him shall say, Where is he?" [7]. This usually happens when the life of the hypocrite is exposed by all men in the end, to be an object of eternal judgment...

20.6.4.en: Those who saw him active in their days will say of him at his death: where is he? For he is no longer seen here, where he used to go about at large, nor is he found in the eternal rest where he was expected to be...

20.6.6.en: * Observe these proud, reckless people, observe the ox being prepared for slaughter, left to roam in freedom, destroying what it wishes, until the day of its slaughter... Scripture refers to it elsewhere as a sacrifice, and says that it is left to an evil freedom (Prov 7:22).

20.6.7.en: * These flourish in the prosperity of this world, and perish by the power of God. They do not perish in the very thing in which they flourish; for they flourish for a time and perish eternally. They flourish in unreal goods and perish in real torments.

20.7.0.en: St. Augustine He shall fly away as a dream, and shall not be found: yea, he shall be chased away as a vision of the night [8].

20.7.1.en: He passes away with all the greatness, wealth and honour he has attained, and he is like a dream which a man searches for on waking and finds no trace of it; he becomes like a phantom that passed and has no existence!

20.7.2.en: * Such, my brethren, is our life, we who live a temporal life. Such is the game we play on earth. We came into being from nothing, and after we exist we dissolve. We are dreams without substance, visions not grasped, like a bird that passes and flies, and like a ship that leaves no trace on the sea (Wis 5:10-11); we are a speck of dust, a vapour, the morning dew, a flower that grows in a moment and in a moment withers. The days of man are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth (Ps 15:103).

20.7.3.en: Well did David, inspired by the Spirit, discuss our weakness, and say: [Make me to know the measure of my days](g), and he knew that the days of man are as a handbreadth (Job 39:4-5).

20.7.4.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus * It is like a dream or a vision of the night. Zophar abuses Job with the same impudence.

20.7.5.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * What is the life of the hypocrite but a vision of fantasy (daydreams) that appears in an outward show and possesses nothing in truth? Therefore it is justly likened to a dream, since every praise or glory is as though it had left him.

20.7.6.en: Often in "the vision of the night" some poor people are amazed to become rich, they see honours poured upon them, they see heaps of wealth, and crowds attending, garments of great beauty, and an abundance of food served to them... But suddenly, when they awake, they find the emptiness of all the joy they were feeling, and they grieve that they awoke, since real need forces them to wake. So it is with the minds of hypocrites: what they do is one thing, and what they appear to be before men is another... and while they are praised by men to excess, they think that what they delight in makes them famous among their fellow creatures.

20.7.8.en: * The Lord teaches us that whoever gives himself over to shameful works is stripped of a garment that is not made of wool but of living virtue, for the garment of virtue is eternal, not temporal.

20.8.0.en: St. Ambrose The eye also which saw him shall see him no more; neither shall his place any more behold him [9].

20.8.1.en: Those who saw him as a very prominent figure, successful, rich and powerful, no longer see him. They look for him where he used to be, and behold, the place is completely empty of him.

20.8.2.en: * Although Zophar says this concerning all the wicked without referring to anyone, it is clear that he refers to Job in all his words. For the "eye" of his other friends and acquaintances left him in contempt, even though (their eyes) had seen beforehand all that was in the beginning, even when they look at him again.

20.8.3.en: "His place" means those who were originally with him in "his place," and from his country, no longer recognize him. For they see the extent of his prolonged sorrows and are struck dumb.

20.8.4.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * What is the "place" of the hypocrite but the heart of those who flatter him? For he rests in the place where he finds those who love him... But as long as he lives he does not cease to teach his followers the very things he practises, and through the boldness of his sinful way he begets others also after the pattern of his own false deceit.

20.8.6.en: Evils remove a man from his place of rest, so that he becomes as though he did not exist. This is what happened with Korah and his company, who in their wickedness presumed against the divine commandment and wanted to seize the priesthood by force, and the earth swallowed them up, and they became as though they did not exist (Num 16:32).

20.8.7.en: * (Concerning Korah, Dathan and Abiram) They separated themselves from the holy congregation. The earth swallowed them alive, as a visible symbol of the invisible punishment.

20.9.0.en: 10 His children shall seek to please the poor, and his hands shall restore their goods. 11 His bones are full of the sin of his youth, which shall lie down with him in the dust. 12 Though wickedness be sweet in his mouth, though he hide it under his tongue; 13 Though he spare it, and forsake it not; but keep it still within his mouth: 14 Yet his meat in his bowels is turned, it is the gall of asps within him. 15 He hath swallowed down riches, and he shall vomit them up again: God shall cast them out of his belly. 16 He shall suck the poison of asps: the viper's tongue shall slay him. 17 He shall not see the rivers, the floods, the brooks of honey and butter. 18 That which he laboured for shall he restore, and shall not swallow it down: according to his substance shall the restitution be, and he shall not rejoice therein. 19 Because he hath oppressed and hath forsaken the poor; because he hath violently taken away an house which he builded not; 20 Surely he shall not feel quietness in his belly, he shall not save of that which he desired. 21 There shall none of his meat be left; therefore shall no man look for his goods. 22 In the fulness of his sufficiency he shall be in straits: every hand of the wicked shall come upon him. 23 When he is about to fill his belly, God shall cast the fury of his wrath upon him, and shall rain it upon him while he is eating. 24 He shall flee from the iron weapon, and the bow of steel shall strike him through. 25 It is drawn, and cometh out of the body; yea, the glittering sword cometh out of his gall: terrors are upon him. 26 All darkness shall be hid in his secret places: a fire not blown shall consume him; it shall go ill with him that is left in his tabernacle. 27 The heaven shall reveal his iniquity; and the earth shall rise up against him. 28 The increase of his house shall depart, and his goods shall flow away in the day of his wrath. 29 This is the portion of a wicked man from God, and the heritage appointed unto him by God.

20.9.1.en: His children shall seek to please the poor, and his hands shall restore their goods [10].

20.9.2.en: Here he gives us examples of the evils that the hypocrite commits in secret in this world, and the punishment they bring upon him:

20.9.3.en: * "May the lowly ones destroy his sons" [10 LXX]. Perhaps Zophar in this manner refers to the demons, for they are "lowly" in relation to human beings, because of their fall from on high. For these are the ones who shattered and destroyed the house in which Job's children died (Job 1:19).

20.9.4.en: "And his hands kindle the fires of sorrow" when Job was scraping his sores with a potsherd.

20.9.5.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * "His sons seek to please the poor." It is written: [Wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul] (Wis 1:4). And the psalmist declares: [The rich have lacked, and suffer hunger] (Ps 34:10). So the sons of the hypocrite [fall down in want] (Job 20:10), because those who are born in hypocrisy in superficiality, since they do not receive the substance of truth, become nothing, suffering from poverty of heart.

20.9.6.en: [And his hands restore his sorrow]. What does he mean by hands but works? So his hands restore his sorrow, because he reaps a just eternal judgment from his evil life.

20.9.8.en: * If anyone says that he does not want the Kingdom of God but seeks only eternal rest, he deceives himself. For there are two places and no third. If someone is not made worthy to reign with Christ, he will surely perish with the devil.

20.10.0.en: 11 His bones are full of the sin of his youth, which shall lie down with him in the dust. 12 Though wickedness be sweet in his mouth, though he hide it under his tongue; 13 Though he spare it, and forsake it not; but keep it still within his mouth: 14 Yet his meat in his bowels is turned, it is the gall of asps within him.

20.10.1.en: His bones are full of the sin of his youth (strength), which shall lie down with him in the dust [11].

20.10.2.en: He falls into the youthful passions that fill his bones, and they hold him and do not leave him until the day of his death.

20.10.3.en: * (Zophar thinks that) the corruption that issues from Job corrupts his bones with the decay of his body, and so spoils the beauty of Job's "youth." His bones sleep with him in the dust, for Job becomes dust from the pus and the dung of the dunghill where he was cast.

20.10.4.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * What is the "youth" of the hypocrite but the beginning of the evil of his youth, when he longed and desired to embrace the passion of glory?... What he began with evil he increases daily and is strengthened through evil habit... Therefore it is written in Proverbs: "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it" (Prov 22:6). These very bones lie down with him in the dust, because evil practices continue with him until they draw him down to the dust of death.

20.10.6.en: * The body in itself is not an obstacle, but rather because of our wickedness we cannot inherit the Kingdom of God.

20.11.0.en: St. John Chrysostom Though wickedness be sweet in his mouth, though he hide it under his tongue [12].

20.11.1.en: He finds the passions sweet, so evil becomes sweet in his mouth, and he hides it under his tongue so that the pleasure may not leave him, as the choicest thing he finds.

20.11.2.en: * "Though wickedness be sweet in his mouth... but he cannot sustain it" [12]. In this statement Job is warned. He means that Job finds his wickedness sweet by his words, in other words, he covers it and hides it by his style, by the words with which he expresses himself... Thus he cannot sustain himself. Because of the evils that have come upon him he appears as a wicked man; and he rebukes him, since he wishes to hide his conduct from outside, and has not considered that it is impossible to hide it.

20.11.3.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * "When evil becomes sweet in his mouth, he hides it under his tongue" [12]. Evil is sweet in the mouth of the hypocrite, since he finds evil sweet in his thought. For the mouth of the heart is the thought, as it is written: [Flattering lips speak with a double heart] (Ps 12:2). Now the sweet evil in the mouth of the hypocrite is hidden under the tongue, since the violence of evil conduct lies hidden in the mind, concealed under the soft garment of the mind...

20.11.5.en: * Sins harm the soul with greater gravity than worms harm the body. And yet we do not perceive their corruption, nor do we feel the urgent need of being cleansed from them. It is like the drunkard who cannot tell how loathsome the taste of the wine is, while the sober man can easily discern it. So with sins: whoever lives soberly easily discerns the mire and corruption, but whoever lives in evil is like one drunk with strong drink and does not realize that he is sick. This is the worst thing about sin, that it does not allow those who fall into it to perceive the state of grave sickness they are in, but they are like those who lie in the mud and think that they are enjoying perfumes. They have not the slightest desire to be set free. And while the worms work in them, they boast like those who have precious stones. Therefore they do not want to kill (sin), but to revive it and multiply it until it carries them across to the worm in the life to come.

20.12.0.en: St. John Chrysostom Though he spare it, and forsake it not; but keep it still within his mouth [13].

20.12.1.en: If pleasure takes hold of him he hides it within him, as one who keeps it shut under his tongue. He is like the harlot of whom it was said: "Yet she multiplied her whoredoms, in calling to remembrance the days of her youth, wherein she had played the harlot" (Ezek 23:19).

20.12.2.en: Hiding the pleasure and keeping it under the tongue shows the effort he makes to conceal his desire, which is very dear to him.

20.12.3.en: But He who knows what is in the heart and the thought also knows what the wicked man hides, the pleasure he hides under his tongue.

20.12.4.en: * [He spares it, and forsakes it not, but keeps it within his throat] [13]. He spares the evil in which he delights. Since he does not practise repentance, it hunts him within. Therefore it is also added: [and forsakes it not], for if he had any thought of leaving it, he would not spare it but would pursue it closely. Now [he keeps it within his throat], for he holds it back in his thought, and will never utter it in his speech.

20.12.6.en: Yet his meat in his bowels is turned!

20.13.0.en: It is the gall of asps within him [14].

20.13.1.en: Since passion becomes his daily food that fills his bowels, it turns into a deadly poison in his depths. While he thinks that in pleasure lies the secret of his life and happiness, and that without it he has no life, behold, it strikes him dead with its poison that he hid within him.

20.13.2.en: * "His meat in his bowels is turned into the gall of asps within him" [14]. Zophar calls the poison of evil "the gall of the asp," for when the gall of the asp spreads in the bowels it can no longer be avoided, for it kills the one in whose bowels it spreads. This is plain and known to all. So the poison of evil works in all who conceal it.

20.13.3.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * There are two kinds of food, one that serves salvation, and the other that suits the perishing... It is fitting that we not misuse the Father's gifts... let us use them in detachment and keep them under our control. Surely we were commanded to be masters and lords of food and not its slaves.

20.13.4.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * Bread in the belly is like being filled with earthly pleasures in the mind. Therefore let the hypocrite now be completely filled with the praise that he cannot resist! Let him revel in honours!

20.13.5.en: "His meat in his bowels is turned into the gall of asps" [14], because fullness with temporal pleasures turns on the day of final judgment into bitterness, so what passes here as praise of greatness is revealed to be "the gall of asps," that is, the swelling pride of evil spirits... The joy of temporal pleasure is sweet when it is tasted here by the chewing of the teeth, but it turns into bitterness in the belly when the joy passes and is swallowed to the destruction of the person.

20.14.0.en: 15 He hath swallowed down riches, and he shall vomit them up again: God shall cast them out of his belly. 16 He shall suck the poison of asps: the viper's tongue shall slay him.

20.14.1.en: He hath swallowed down riches, and he shall vomit them up again.

20.14.2.en: God shall cast them out of his belly [15].

20.14.3.en: In his love for the world he gathers riches and stores them, like one who swallows food greedily because he is hungry. There is in him no sufficiency or fullness, but it is said: "The horseleach hath two daughters, crying, Give, give. There are three things that are never satisfied, yea, four things say not, It is enough" (Prov 30:15). He is like one who fills his stomach, but constantly vomits up all that he ate, so that he remains hungry continually.

20.14.4.en: * "The wealth gathered unjustly he will vomit up"... For it is impossible to make amends without harm... the reward of the wicked is kept for the life to come (Col 3:25). Therefore what is gathered unjustly he will vomit up with great cries and great ruin of the soul, when the wealth gathered unjustly is demanded for judgment.

20.14.5.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * The hypocrite desires to know the revelations of God, but does not practise them. He wants to speak wisdom, but does not live wisely. Therefore, since he does not practise what he knows he ought to do, he loses even what he knows. Since he does not join pure practice to his knowledge, despising the purity of true practice, he loses the knowledge itself. Therefore the wealth of the holy Law that he "swallowed" by reading, he vomits up by forgetting it, and God casts it out of his belly. In this, since he does not care to keep the practice, by a just judgment God uproots it from his memory, so that he refrains from keeping the commandments of God on his tongue, as long as he does not keep them in his life. So it was said by the prophet: "But unto the wicked God saith, What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or that thou shouldest take my covenant in thy mouth?" (Ps 50:16).

20.14.7.en: * The wicked are scattered in bitterness (like light chaff), while the righteous are saved like heavy wheat. Therefore notice what the Lord says to Peter: "Behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: but I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not" (Lk 22:31-32). Those who are scattered like chaff perish, but he who does not perish is like the seed that falls and grows and increases and brings forth much fruit (Lk 8:8)... Evil is likened to chaff, which burns quickly and turns to dust.

20.14.8.en: St. Ambrose He shall suck the poison of asps.

20.15.0.en: The viper's tongue shall slay him [16].

20.15.1.en: As the hypocrite draws from the love of the world, he sucks the poison of serpents against which no charm avails, and than which nothing is more deadly and fatal. This is what the lover of the world gathers for himself. He takes into his depths the serpent of sin, which kills him with its tongue.

20.15.2.en: * "The viper's tongue also shall slay him" [16]. This is he who from the beginning subjected Adam and Eve (Gen 3:4-5), and now does not cease to enslave sinners, teaching them to find pleasure in evil deeds.

20.15.3.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * "He shall suck the poison of asps: the viper's tongue shall slay him" [16]... For at first (the unclean spirit) steals into them gently, but afterward he drags them away violently. So "he shall suck the poison of asps" where at first a hidden suggestion is offered that arises in the heart, but "the viper's tongue shall slay him" where afterward he kills the captive soul with the poison of violent temptation. Pope Gregory (the Great)

20.16.0.en: 17 He shall not see the rivers, the floods, the brooks of honey and butter. 18 That which he laboured for shall he restore, and shall not swallow it down: according to his substance shall the restitution be, and he shall not rejoice therein.

20.16.1.en: He shall not see the rivers, the floods, the brooks of honey and butter [17].

20.16.2.en: * They do not see the gain from the flock that is pastured, and they do not receive milk and butter in the age to come. For they cannot enjoy pleasure in the things in which they boast here. For the instruction of such, the words of the Lord are fitting: [Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?] (Lk 12:20).

20.16.3.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * [He shall not see the brooks of the river of honey and the rushing butter] [17]. The Lord says in the Gospel: "He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water" (Jn 7:38). And the Evangelist continues: "(But this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive.)" So the "channels of the river" are the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Love is a channel of the river, and faith is a channel of the river, and hope is a channel of the river. But no hypocrite loves God or his neighbour when he makes the glory of the world his goal, therefore he does not see the channels of the river, since he is not watered by the overflow of love.

20.16.4.en: The only-begotten Son of the Most High Father, who is God over all, became man among all, and, supplying us with the sweetness of His divine nature and the mystery of His incarnation, satisfied us with honey and butter.

20.16.6.en: Evils offer honey and milk or butter, hiding deadly poison. But our Christ, who forgives sins, offered us the honey of sweet peace, our inner peace with ourselves as with God and His angels and His saints. Deliverance from sin by the work of redemption restores us not to the garden of Eden with Adam and Eve, nor to Canaan that flows with milk and honey, but to surpassing reconciliation with heaven.

20.16.7.en: * Whoever seeks peace seeks Christ, for He is our peace (Col 1:20), who maketh both one (Eph 2:14), making peace by the blood of His cross, whether on earth or in heaven.

20.16.8.en: St. Basil the Great * The earth was split from heaven, and the angels became enemies to men, when they saw the Lord insulted by them...

20.16.9.en: What Christ did on the Cross was to lift up to heaven the (sinful) human nature that was in bondage to the evil one. Thus in fact He brought the enemy hated by the angels. Not only did He make what is on earth to be at peace, but He brought to them the one who had been their enemy. By this the peace became very deep. The angels appeared again on earth, because humanity on its part appeared in heaven.

20.17.0.en: St. John Chrysostom That which he laboured for shall he restore, and shall not swallow it down: according to his substance (and the gain of his merchandise) he shall not rejoice therein [18].

20.17.1.en: He expects to draw from the world as from brooks and channels that flow honey and milk, so he does not cease working night and day to store up the riches of the world. But soon he finds that he is poor, that he does not possess what he hoped for, and joy does not steal into him, for he finds no happiness in all that he has acquired.

20.17.2.en: Whoever gathers money unjustly returns what he gathered, willingly or unwillingly, so that nothing remains with him, but he becomes destitute.

20.17.3.en: * "He labours in vain and without profit, who clings to the wealth that he shall not taste" [18 LXX]. What is the use of the grandeur of a palace dripping with gold if the wicked man himself is buried six feet under (the earth)? What is the use of a multitude of festive garments and a variety of clothing to a person whom the worms strip?

20.17.4.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem The wicked man will discover that he came out of the world naked, because he does not put on Christ Himself, our righteousness. And his nakedness will be exposed on the day of judgment, and he will go off with the enemy of good, who stripped himself and his angels and his followers among the sons of men. All have lost what covered them with joy!

20.17.5.en: * His garment was taken from him (Joseph) (Gen 39:12), but he was not naked, because he was still covered with the garment of purity.

20.17.6.en: No one is naked except the man whose guilt is exposed.

20.17.7.en: In the first times we have this truth, that Adam, when he disobeyed the commandment of God and became indebted by a grave sin, became naked; for this reason he said: "I heard thy voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself" (Gen 3:10). Adam affirms that he is naked because he lost the adornment of divine protection. And he hid because he had not the garment of faith, which he cast aside by his disobedience.

20.17.8.en: You see an important truth: Adam was naked although he had not lost his robe, and Joseph had his garments taken from him, which he left in the hand of the adulteress, and was not naked.

20.18.0.en: Because he hath oppressed and hath forsaken the poor; because he hath violently taken away an house which he builded not [19].

20.18.1.en: In his love for the world he walks in a spirit of cruelty and injustice, so he crushes the poor and leaves them, and plunders houses and seizes them for himself, as Ahab seized the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, and so seized for himself death and shame.

20.18.2.en: When covetousness masters a man, not only does he not give from what he has to those in need, but he takes what belongs to another, so he breaks into the houses of the poor and strips them; he is not ashamed to shatter them by violence.

20.18.3.en: Whoever gives alms from money by which he wronged his brethren carries in his almsgiving neither spiritual love nor even human love, for he gives to one man and wrongs another.

20.18.4.en: * If you offer to God a part of what you acquired unjustly and by seizure, God will not accept your gift...

20.18.5.en: Rather have mercy on the one you wronged, doing him mercy and love, acting with goodness, and thereby you offer mercy and truth. For God does not share in our greed, nor does He share with robbers and plunderers; He is able to feed the poor whom He entrusted to us, but He seeks the fruits of righteousness and love for men.

20.18.6.en: Pope Athanasius the Apostolic * If you have seized money and given it to others... what is your excuse?

20.18.7.en: Would you know the measure of the evil you do? Hear what Solomon says, that whoever offers a sacrifice from the goods of the poor is like one who kills his son before his father's eyes!

20.19.0.en: 20 Surely he shall not feel quietness in his belly, he shall not save of that which he desired. 21 There shall none of his meat be left; therefore shall no man look for his goods. 22 In the fulness of his sufficiency he shall be in straits: every hand of the wicked shall come upon him. 23 When he is about to fill his belly, God shall cast the fury of his wrath upon him, and shall rain it upon him while he is eating. 24 He shall flee from the iron weapon, and the bow of steel shall strike him through. 25 It is drawn, and cometh out of the body; yea, the glittering sword cometh out of his gall: terrors are upon him. 26 All darkness shall be hid in his secret places: a fire not blown shall consume him; it shall go ill with him that is left in his tabernacle. 27 The heaven shall reveal his iniquity; and the earth shall rise up against him. 28 The increase of his house shall depart, and his goods shall flow away in the day of his wrath. 29 This is the portion of a wicked man from God, and the heritage appointed unto him by God.

20.19.1.en: Surely he shall not feel quietness in his belly, he shall not save of that which he desired [20].

20.19.2.en: In all his unceasing striving his depths (his belly) know no peace of mind (contentment), but anxiety besieges him and masters him. He may obtain much, but he himself is not saved.

20.19.3.en: * We must control the belly and keep it under the direction of heaven. For God will in the end destroy all that belongs to the belly, as the Apostle says.

20.20.0.en: St. Clement of Alexandria There shall none of his meat be left; therefore shall no man look for his goods [21].

20.20.1.en: What he obtained flees from him, like one who eats but is not satisfied by the food because he vomits it up...

20.20.2.en: * Because the wicked man eats without giving thanks (Rom 14:6), tastes without blessing, and the poor man has no place at his table (Lk 16:21). [He has no provision] [21]. Since the wicked man has no remnant, David himself adds: [The remnant of the wicked shall be utterly destroyed].

20.20.3.en: [His goods do not last]; why? Because his goods have no root, and they produce evil fruits.

20.20.4.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * "His goods do not last"... because he runs after everything and does not fear the Judge, and when he departs from this life he goes naked to the Judge.

20.21.0.en: In the fulness of his sufficiency he shall be in straits.

20.21.1.en: Every hand of the wicked shall come upon him [22].

20.21.2.en: After Zophar described the perplexities that befall the cruel oppressor, he shows his complete ruin. For with obtaining what he desired in one way or another, the hands of the wretched turn to his paths. What he did is done to him. As his hand was unjust upon others, the hands of the wicked are stretched out against him.

20.21.3.en: * [In the fulness of his sufficiency he shall be in straits] [22]. First he runs panting to heap up the things he gathers by covetousness, and when he has gathered very much, as in the belly of covetousness, "in the fulness of his sufficiency he shall be in straits," for he is filled with anxiety about how to keep what he has obtained, so his fullness becomes the subject of his distress. When the field of a certain rich man brought forth a great harvest, and he had no place to store it, he said: [What shall I do, because I have no room where to bestow my fruits? And he said, This will I do: I will pull down my barns, and build greater] (Lk 12:17-18). So this man, who was in straits with abundance of goods, said: "What shall I do?" He was in care, as though the multitude of food pressed upon him.

20.21.4.en: * "He is burned with the heat, and every woe falls upon him" [22]. After acquiring gifts of wealth, he achieves what he desired, and another disturbance comes to him. Fear and anxiety come upon him to keep safe what it cost him boundless troubles to obtain. On every side he is terrified of conspirators, and fears lest what he did to others be done to him. He fears lest he be subjected to violence by someone stronger than he. When he sees a poor man he looks at him as a thief. He fears the very things he has stored up, lest through the weakness of his inherited nature they be lost through neglect. In all these matters, because of the very fear of punishment, the wretched man suffers severely from fear of what he may suffer.

20.21.5.en: But it is a wonderful security for the heart that does not seek what is not ours, but is content with what it receives day by day.
